Function 1: pooled cohort model predictions¶

Side quest — 20 October 2026. A copy of the Week 4 notebook, using 19 observations: 10 shared initial points, 3 confirmed own returns and 6 additional peer records. The original methods and search settings are retained. A separate magnitude-target comparison tests the activity hypothesis alongside the signed models. Peer data are published reports, not independently verified portal returns. See the dataset audit for exact sources and exclusions.

Week 4 has already been submitted. Any original coverage plan is a historical reference; any newly calculated suggestion here is hypothetical. This pooled snapshot includes records collected later, so its validation is not a forecast made before the original Week 3 return. Query-budget numbers refer to the original start of Week 4 and confer no additional evaluation allowance.

Function description and modelling clues¶

Course description, paraphrased. Locate possible contamination sources in a two-input field; the lesson associates non-zero readings with proximity. Maximise the supplied signed output.

Source: Mini-lesson 12.8: function descriptions, reviewed 20 October 2026. The notes below interpret the fixed cohort snapshot collected on that date. Peer outputs are published reports, not independently verified portal returns. Every official objective remains maximisation of signed y.

Read the cohort evidence and exploration clues alongside these model results.

What the fitted comparisons add¶

The separate activity target is $$g(y)=\log_{10}(1+|y|/10^{-200})=|h(y)|.$$ It folds measured negative targets upwards before refitting, retaining the existing log compression. It is not the absolute value of an old fitted surface. The magnitude fits form a broader central band of predicted activity; the quadratic and the two GP length scales still disagree about its detailed shape.

The broad magnitude GP has the lowest held-out error: 31.9% of its own mean baseline MAE, versus 96.0% for the preferred signed GP. These ratios compare predictability of different targets; they do not establish better signed-score prediction or validate the source hypothesis.

On the common candidate pool, the magnitude broad-GP UCB point is (0.563545, 0.515620), only about 0.025 from an observation. It refines a known central neighbourhood. The local magnitude GP suggests the less-sampled south-west extension (0.321717, 0.357282) instead. Its weight-3 proposal moves to a boundary corner through uncertainty, not measured evidence for another source.

Held-out comparisons and method selection use the same small snapshot; they are not independent final-test results. The notes do not change targets, settings or query policies.

2. Learn the picture before using it on the black box¶

The blue line is the GP's posterior mean: its central prediction after seeing observations. The pale band is mean plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations: a pointwise interval for the latent function under the model's assumptions. It is not a simultaneous guarantee for the whole curve, and it excludes fresh observation noise. Green crosses are measured values at the displayed inputs.

Only in this invented one-input example can we also draw the orange dashed known function. The three panels use 3, 6 and 10 points from a fixed invented sequence. They demonstrate updating a model, not a query-selection policy. None of these points uses the course query allowance. The GP's kernel, noise level and prior scale stay fixed across the panels.

The same visual convention is used in scikit-learn's introductory GP example. For the actual black box we have observations and predictions, but no known orange truth curve.

3. Choose what the model is predicting¶

Function 1 mixes signs and spans roughly 197 orders of magnitude. A raw-output fit would mainly respond to the two large negative magnitudes. Retain the signed-log height used in exploration:

$$h(y) = \operatorname{sign}(y)\log_{10}(1 + |y| / s), \qquad s = 10^{-200}.$$

This fixed plotting convention preserves signs and ordering; it changes distances and the errors that fitting tries to minimise. We declare s once and do not tune it using validation. Held-out checks below assess prediction on this fixed transformed scale, not the full process of choosing a transformation or prediction accuracy in raw output units.

Every GP mean, standard deviation and score below is in height units h. Transforming a GP mean back would not give the mean raw output. The original CSV and y remain unchanged.

4. State competing models, then hide one result at a time¶

  • Mean baseline: ignore the inputs and predict the training outputs' average height.
  • Linear ridge: fit a tilted plane, with a penalty that restrains large coefficients.
  • Quadratic ridge: add x1², x1*x2 and x2², allowing broad curvature and an interaction.
  • Local GP: assume nearby inputs share information over an RBF length scale of 0.15.
  • Broad GP: repeat with length scale 0.35, sharing information over larger distances.

Both ridge penalties are fixed at alpha=1.0. The GP noise SD is assumed to be 10% of the training height SD. Targets are normalised inside each GP fit; feature scaling for ridge is also refitted inside each training fold. The GP settings are declared teaching assumptions, not fitted truths or the result of a hyperparameter search.

Leave-one-out (LOO) means each prediction hides its own observation and trains on the other 18. Lower MAE or RMSE is better. MAE / baseline < 1 beats the mean on this small-sample check. Training error shows how well a model represents points it has already seen; it is not the same evidence.

5. Repeat the prediction picture: vary x1, hold x2 fixed¶

Use the best observed input as a reference location. Vary x1 and hold its x2 coordinate fixed. This makes a one-dimensional slice through the two-input model. The left panel shows that path; its dotted boundary encloses the sampled inputs. The right repeats the blue mean, pale band and green measurements from the toy example.

Only measurements whose x2 actually matches the held value appear as green crosses on this curve. Other observations still influence the joint GP; they remain on the input map rather than being falsely projected onto the slice. The curve spans the full input interval, so parts outside the sampled boundary are extrapolations.

Use the local GP for this illustration; it is not automatically the best model in the validation table. A narrow band expresses this model's confidence, which can still be misplaced if its assumptions are wrong.

The three real-data curve pictures share vertical limits, so their apparent heights and band widths can be compared directly.

Reference input: x1=0.540351, x2=0.524565; observed y=1.180859e-13
Local GP held-out MAE / baseline: 0.96

6. Repeat it again: vary x2, hold x1 fixed¶

Now move in the other input direction through the same reference point. The model and observations are unchanged; only the path through the input square changes. Read the same three elements again: mean, model band and measurements actually on the slice. Differences between the two curves describe the fitted input relationship, not a known property of the black box.

7. Change an assumption, then repeat the first slice¶

Return to varying x1, now with the broad GP. Its larger length scale shares information between more distant inputs. Compare this picture with Section 5 and compare their held-out errors in Section 4. An appealing smooth curve is not evidence by itself. The band reflects the chosen kernel and noise assumptions; it does not include uncertainty about which model or target transformation is appropriate.

The GP noise parameter and returned standard deviation follow the GaussianProcessRegressor documentation.

Both GPs can overshoot the measured height range between observations or outside the sampled region. On this chosen transform, h = 200 corresponds approximately to raw y = 1; substantially larger heights would imply enormous raw values compared with the current observations. These are unconstrained model outputs, not evidence that such a peak exists. Smoothness and a narrow band do not resolve this target-scale sensitivity.

8. From curves to contour maps¶

A curve examined one path. A contour joins locations in the input square with the same fitted height. Its number is a height h, not a raw output, observation rank or uncertainty. Closer contours indicate a steeper change in the fitted mean. The colours fill the bands between levels.

The quadratic from the earlier exploration experiment and the local GP now predict on the same regular grid. The panels share colour limits and contour levels. Coloured dots are observations on that same height scale; colour differences between a dot and its background expose a fitting mismatch. Blank regions are outside the sampled convex hull; interior gaps still have model uncertainty. The right map shows a GP mean, not its uncertainty. Keep the validation table in view when interpreting either surface.

9. Separate a high prediction from high uncertainty¶

Read the next panels from left to right: the GP mean, its standard deviation, then an illustrative upper confidence bound:

$$\operatorname{UCB}(x) = \mu(x) + \kappa\sigma(x), \qquad \kappa = 1.96.$$

A high UCB can come from a promising mean, substantial uncertainty, or both. It is an acquisition score, not a predicted output or a guarantee of improvement. The weight is a declared heuristic. Its numerical agreement with the band multiplier does not prove an optimal policy.

Here the full input square is coloured so uncertainty outside the sampled hull is visible. The dotted outline marks that hull; coloured areas outside it are explicit extrapolations. Each panel has its own units and colour scale. The gold star remains the next saved coverage point, rather than a model-selected replacement. The table evaluates the remaining coverage inputs without changing their order.

10. If we switched today: a hypothetical model-led next query¶

Choose the lower-LOO-MAE GP among the two fixed GP comparisons, then maximise mean + 1.96 * SD over a declared finite candidate pool. A GP supplies both the mean and uncertainty needed for this rule; the lowest-error model overall may still be a different regressor. This is a transparent counterfactual policy, not proof that the GP or its settings are optimal. Selecting a model using these same 19 observations can make its reported error optimistic.

The pool contains 4,096 seeded Sobol points plus the four allowed extreme corners. Round inputs to six decimals before predicting, remove duplicates and already observed coordinates, then score those exact inputs. The winner is the best of this finite pool, not a proven continuous optimum. Candidates outside the sampled hull are permitted and explicitly labelled as extrapolations.

The table reports a single suggested input, its posterior mean, standard deviation and UCB in the model's target units. A second table changes only the exploration weight, reusing the same predictions. Weight zero chooses the highest mean. The magenta X marks the hypothetical query; the gold star remains the saved coverage choice. No new course evaluation is made, and the original Week 4 reference plan remains unchanged.

The chosen GP's MAE ratio is printed beside the suggestion. A ratio of 1 or more means it does not beat the mean baseline; the hypothetical query then lacks even that predictive support.

11. Target sensitivity: what if negative outputs count as zero?¶

Consider a separate modelling question:

$$y_+ = \max(y, 0), \qquad h_+ = \log_{10}(1 + y_+ / s).$$

Ten negative observations share a zero baseline; nine positives keep their original heights. Keep all 19 rows and refit the same quadratic. Floor negative fitted heights at zero for both plotting and held-out checks. This floor is explicit post-processing, not a non-negativity constraint on the quadratic's coefficients.

The target and error scale have changed. Comparing a new error number with the original MAE would not establish better prediction of the original outputs. Nothing here establishes that the negative measurements were wrong. The CSV, original target and coverage plan are preserved.

Activity hypothesis: predict absolute magnitude¶

The cohort exploration asks whether both signs indicate activity. Here we refit the same five methods to a second target:

$$g(y)=\log_{10}(1+|y|/s)=|h(y)|,\qquad s=10^{-200}.$$

This retains the previous log compression across almost 200 orders of magnitude. It folds each measured negative value upwards before fitting; it is not the absolute value of the old fitted surface. Every non-zero output contributes, without inventing a detection threshold. Large negative outputs now count as strong activity, whereas the course still rewards the highest signed output.

Inputs, observations, leave-one-out folds, model settings and candidate pool stay the same. Neither target is clipped. Compare each target with its own mean baseline: a lower error for g does not establish better signed-score prediction, source detection or distance estimation.

What happens to the fitted shape?¶

Read across each row to change the target while holding the method fixed. The signed surfaces must turn between large negative and positive heights at nearby inputs. The magnitude surfaces can join those readings into a broader high-activity region. Shared colours and axes make the upward fold visible. The quadratic and the two GPs still impose different shapes. The magnitude quadratic retains a north-east emphasis; the local GP favours a smaller south-west peak, while the broad GP joins them into a central band. The local signed GP also overshoots into deep troughs between measurements: those extremes are predictions, not additional observed readings.

The cross-sections then hold x2 at the best signed observation's coordinate in both fits. Their bands describe the declared GP assumptions; they are not probabilities of a source being present.

Score the same finite pool used above, with all coordinates rounded before prediction. Compare each GP with itself under h and g, then consider the GP with the lowest held-out error for each target. This separates the effect of changing the target from the effect of changing the preferred length scale.

What this identifies in the pooled snapshot¶

  • Central follow-up: the preferred magnitude GP (GP: broad (l=0.35)) has its finite-pool mean peak at (0.532449, 0.525216). Adding the standard uncertainty allowance moves it to (0.563545, 0.515620). This is close to the strong signed return, in the region also containing large negative readings. It is a local follow-up for examining the sign transition and activity hypothesis.
  • South-west extension: the shorter-scale magnitude GP suggests (0.321717, 0.357282), about 0.144 from the nearest observation. That is an alternative, more sparsely measured area, dependent on the kernel assumption.
  • Changed emphasis: the signed-target policy suggested (0.690526, 0.410029). Magnitude shifts attention towards and to the south-west of the central negative cluster, whose strongest observed |y| is at (0.419675, 0.463269).

The magnitude GP's held-out MAE is 31.9% of its own mean baseline, compared with 96.0% for the preferred signed GP. The folded target is easier to predict in this sample. Both targets were assessed on the same small snapshot used to choose between methods; these are not independent test results.

The central UCB point is only 0.025 from the nearest observation. It refines a known neighbourhood rather than opening an unexplored part of the square. Magnitude targets are non-negative, but these unconstrained models can still predict below zero near the boundary.

The local GP's weight-3 magnitude proposal moves to an unobserved boundary corner. That is uncertainty-driven extrapolation, not evidence for another source. None of these fits establishes a shared source, an ECG-like response, or that large magnitude is close to a source. A magnitude query can return a very negative value and perform poorly on the signed maximisation objective.

Read the pictures in the same order each time¶

  1. Identify the input path or plane, target scale and measured observations.
  2. Read the fitted mean before looking at its band or contour colours.
  3. Name the assumptions behind the uncertainty and check hidden-result errors against the mean baseline.
  4. Separate a predicted response from an acquisition score and the actual query policy.

The working evidence is a small comparison on 19 observations. Reusing these observations to choose among models can make the winning error optimistic. No picture supplies the unknown true surface or proves that a predicted optimum is real. The exploration notebook's original coverage sequence records the submitted Week 4 decision; these model studies provide practice and hypotheses to revisit with future observations.
